text: This lab pulls together everything from this chapter — the opaque Qubit type and use allocation, the operation-function split, intrinsic gates, and functors — into one small, concrete piece of code you build yourself: a reusable state-preparation operation, undone by its own compiler-generated Adjoint, and verified by measurement.

Four steps hold the whole lab together: a pure function supplies a fixed rotation angle, the same pattern from Lesson 7 — classical computation stays classical-typed. An operation marked is Adj plus Ctl actually touches the qubit, using that angle. Adjoint undoes it, and you confirm the qubit genuinely returns to |0>. And Controlled applies the whole thing conditionally — with every probability claim along the way hand-verified rather than assumed.

PrepAngle returns pi over 3, sixty degrees, with no qubits involved at all. PrepareState then applies Ry with that angle. Because PrepareState only contains a single intrinsic rotation, and Ry itself supports both functors, the compiler generates a correct Adjoint and Controlled variant automatically — you never write the negated angle by hand, even though that's exactly what the generated adjoint does underneath.

Before trusting what measurement will show, it's worth computing the real numbers. Ry of sixty degrees applied to |0> gives the amplitude vector cosine of thirty degrees, sine of thirty degrees — numerically, 0.866 and 0.5. Squaring those gives the measurement probabilities: P of zero comes out to 0.75, P of one to 0.25. Both numbers come from direct matrix-vector multiplication, confirming PrepareState puts the qubit in a state where measuring zero happens seventy-five percent of the time, over many shots.

PrepareThenUndo applies PrepareState, then Adjoint PrepareState right after — mathematically, Ry of negative sixty degrees following Ry of sixty degrees. Multiplying a rotation by its own inverse gives the identity matrix exactly, with no rounding residue on the |1> amplitude — it comes out as precisely zero. That means M of q returns Zero with probability 1.0, every single time, on an ideal noiseless simulator. You didn't write the undo logic; the verification confirms the compiler's generated inverse is exactly correct.

If ctrl is |0> when ConditionalPrep runs, target stays |0> and measuring it returns Zero with certainty. If ctrl had been flipped to |1> first, target would receive the same Ry rotation from Step 3, with the same 75/25 split. The control qubit's state alone decides which behavior happens — nothing about PrepareState's own code changes.
That closes Chapter 2's operations and data types. Chapter 3 moves from local simulation to the real platform: setting up an actual Azure Quantum workspace, starting with lesson 11.
